item.title: Sri Lanka’s national inflation rises to 41-month high of 8.5-pct in October; transport leads
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Increase in transport prices result in non-food inflation to rise
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s nation-wide inflation index, as measured by the National Consumer Price Index (NCPI) on a year-on-year basis, rose to 8.5 percent in October 2026, up from 8.1 percent a month ago, data from the state statistics office showed.

It stood at its highest since June 2023, official data showed.

The NCPI, an alternative to the widely watched Colombo Consumer Price Index, rose 0.4 percent, in October 2026, registering 225.1 compared to 224.2 in September 2026.

The year-on-year inflation of the food group increased to 7.2 percent in the last month from 6.9 percent in September 2026.

Year-on-year inflation for the non-food group accelerated to 9.5 percent from 9.1 percent a month ago, mainly driven by transport cost after the government raised fuel prices in the end of October.

The NCPI includes 485 items representing consumption of Sri Lanka households. It is compiled three weeks after the end of each month and the release of the key index Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI). (Colombo/October 21/2026)

item.title: Foreign outflows from Sri Lanka rupee bonds continue for fifth straight week
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: Sri Lanka has suffered Rs. 42.5 billion worth foreign outflows from the rupee bonds in last seven weeks.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Foreign investors sold Sri Lanka rupee bonds and exited the island nation’s risk-free assets for a fifth straight week in the week ended on November 18, Central Bank data showed, amid depreciation in the rupee currency.

With the latest outflows, the island nation has seen net foreign selling in seven out of the last 22 weeks.

Offshore investors sold a net Rs. 8,583 million (US$26 million) worth of Sri Lanka rupee bonds in the week ended on November 19.

The net selling extended the net foreign outflows from the rupee bonds to Rs. 42.5 billion in the last seven weeks.

Despite outflows in the last five weeks, the island nation has seen a total inflow of around Rs. 29.6 billion into local currency bonds this year through Nov 19, following a net inflow of 71.5 billion rupees last year.

The latest foreign selling comes after the U.S. mid-term election showed strong checks and balances for Trump’s presidential powers and hopes of an end to hostilities against Iran. It also came as the Israel Prime Minister failed to secure a majority in his election.

The rupee had been steady for more than three years before the sharp depreciation in May with the Central Bank citing higher oil and vehicle imports amid a lingering conflict in the Middle East.

The rupee has fallen 6.9 percent through November 13, this year.

Globally, investors are cautious about economic growth due to the impact of the latest Middle East escalation.

The rupee has stabilized after the Central Bank raised its key monetary policy rate by 100 basis points in May to curb inflationary pressure stemming from higher demand. The Central Bank, siting higher inflationary expectation raised the policy rate by 25 basis points on Friday (20).

The island nation has seen an uptick in inflation in the last seven months following a nearly 50 percent hike in fuel prices.

The government raised fuel prices in the last week of October, raising further inflationary concerns.

Before the May rate hike, the Central Bank kept its key policy rates steady since May 2025 after reducing them by 825 basis points over 24 months since June 2023 and foreign investors have been buying rupee bonds. (Colombo/November 23/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka opens draft labour law reforms for public views, briefs lawmakers
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Allowing members of the public and relevant stakeholders to submit their views and proposals.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka has published the first four chapters of a proposed Labour Standards Bill online to gather public feedback as officials move to review and combine the country’s labour laws.

The drafted chapters are now available on the Ministry of Labour’s official website, labourmin.gov.lk, allowing members of the public and relevant stakeholders to submit their views and proposals.

Ministry of Labour officials briefed Members of Parliament on the planned reforms during a special meeting held at Parliament on November 18.

The session was chaired by Minister Anil Jayantha, Chairman of the Ministerial Consultative Committee on Labour Affairs.

An expert committee appointed with Cabinet approval is formulating the new legal framework to update Sri Lanka’s labour rules for the current and future world of work.

Officials told lawmakers that the main goal is to review existing major labour laws and bring them into one updated framework.

The proposed reforms are being developed under four main areas: labour standards, occupational health and safety, industrial relations and disputes, and trade union rights.

Under the new framework, authorities plan to cover paternity leave, maternity protection, and the prevention of violence and harassment in the workplace.

The proposed provisions also address working hours, leave, overtime, making employment contracts formal, and ensuring a safe working environment.

In addition, the laws will cover social security benefits and the rights of part-time employees.

Ministry officials said views from relevant stakeholders—including trade unions, employers, and employee representatives—are expected to be taken into account while shaping the proposed laws.

Deputy Minister of Labour Mahinda Jayasinghe, Members of Parliament, and a group of officials from the Ministry of Labour also attended the meeting. (Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka urged to fill vacant diplomatic posts in US, China
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: "Sri Lanka is on the world map, but we have to be seen and heard to move forward."
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Opposition legislator Ravi Karunanayake has urged the government to immediately appoint envoys to several key diplomatic posts which are vacant, including in the USA, China and Germany.

“Why haven’t you appointed ambassadors or high commissioners to Washington, Beijing and Berlin? Seychelles, is a small country alright; then there is Jordan which was recently filled,” Karunanayake asked the foreign minister in parliament.

“Even Canada, we have made no appointment. This is a big question.”

America, Germany and China were key he said. “I think you must appoint diplomats to these positions without delay.”

He urged the government to hire productive new recruits to take the ministry forward.

“I won’t ask what the career diplomat ratio here is; what is imperative is appointing smart ambassadors.”

“Also look at the concept of commercial diplomacy. Hon minister you are basically being seen all over. Now that is a necessary ingredient of commercial diplomacy. Ensure that you and the deputy minister take this to the next level.

“Sri Lanka is on the world map, but we have to be seen and heard to move forward.” (Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: ADB approves $200mn loan to boost MSME financing in Sri Lanka
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: $100 million policy-based loan to improve the financial ecosystem for MSMEs and a $100 million financial intermediation
item.content:encoded:
COLOMBO, SRI LANKA — The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a $200 million loan to help Sri Lanka strengthen micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) by expanding access to inclusive finance, reducing credit information gaps, and building resilience to shocks.

The financing package consists of a $100 million policy-based loan to improve the financial ecosystem for MSMEs and a $100 million financial intermediation loan to expand access to investment loans for MSMEs including $40 million for green loans.

“This program will help the Government of Sri Lanka build a stronger, more inclusive financial ecosystem that enables MSMEs to grow, innovate, and withstand economic shocks and disasters related to the changing climate,” said ADB Country Director for Sri Lanka Shannon Cowlin. “By improving access to finance—especially for women entrepreneurs—and expanding green financing, ADB is supporting Sri Lanka’s transition to a more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable financing ecosystem for MSMEs.”

MSMEs are crucial to Sri Lanka’s economy, contributing more than 52% of gross domestic product and 45% of overall employment. However, they continue to be constrained by limited access to finance, low levels of digitalization, and vulnerability to shocks such as disasters related to the changing climate.

The Building a Strong and Inclusive Financial Ecosystem for MSMEs Sector Development Program will address these challenges by expanding financial inclusion through enhanced digitalization, improving equitable access to information for MSMEs, formalizing institutional processes, and enhancing financial literacy.

It will support legal reforms to establish the Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Authority, improve oversight and reduce predatory lending, strengthen credit information systems to reduce information gaps, expand credit guarantees, and advance digital financial infrastructure and consumer protection.

Credit lines will be provided by participating financial institutions to expand green financing for MSMEs engaged in environmentally sustainable investments and activities. The program will help MSMEs—at least 20% of which are owned or led by women—invest in measures to mitigate and adapt to shocks related to the changing climate. It will also support innovative financing mechanisms to help growth-stage SMEs access equity financing.

item.title: Sierra Cables public stake rises to 49.72-pct after Rs1.23bn share sale
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: The 34 million shares held by Iconic Trust were previously excluded from the public holding calculation.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sierra Cables PLC said its public shareholding rose to 49.72 percent after Iconic Trust (Private) Limited sold 34 million voting shares, or a 6.33 percent stake, on the Colombo Stock Exchange for 1.225 billion rupees.

The shares were sold through market deals on November 17, at prices ranging from 36.00 rupees to 37.10 rupees each.

The weighted average price was 36.03 rupees per share, bringing the total value to 1,225,112,430 rupees before transaction costs.

“Sierra Cables PLC wishes to inform the market that its public holding has increased by more than two per centum (2%) from the public holding most recently disclosed to the market,” the company said in a filing.

The 34 million shares held by Iconic Trust were previously excluded from the public holding calculation.

Because public investors bought these shares, the company’s public float jumped by 6.33 percentage points from 43.39 percent on September 30, 2026, triggering a required market disclosure.

Following the sale, Iconic Trust holds 129,580,768 ordinary voting shares, representing a 24.11 percent stake in the company.

“The Company continues to comply with the minimum public holding requirement under Rule 7.12.1(A) of the Listing Rules, under Option 1,” Sierra Cables PLC said in its notice to the CSE.

Sierra Cables directors D S K Amarasekera and M A P N Weerasingha, who are also directors of Iconic Trust, notified the board of the disposal on November 20, in line with the Companies Act and exchange rules.

Their relevant interest through Iconic Trust fell from 163,580,768 shares to 129,580,768 shares.

The announcement was signed by LOLC Corporate Services (Private) Limited as company secretaries.(Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka lawmaker questions central bank rate, SRR hike over debt costs, SME hit
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Before eight days had even passed after the President presented 2027 economic forecasts to Parliament, the Central Bank
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Opposition legislator Ravi Karunanayake questioned the government in Parliament over a surprise central bank interest rate and reserve ratio hike, warning the tightening contradicts earlier inflation assurances and will sharply raise state debt costs.

Deputy Minister of Finance Anil Jayantha Fernando put off answering by requesting time to obtain answers from relevant institutions.

Karunanayake noted that on August 1, the Central Bank Governor told Reuters that inflation would peak near July’s 7.3 percent and no further rate hikes would be needed in 2026.

However, the Colombo Consumer Price Index inflation climbed to 8.3 percent in October.

Following a 100-basis-point increase in May, the monetary authority raised its Overnight Policy Rate by 25 basis points to 9 percent on November 20 and hiked the Statutory Reserve Ratio from 2 percent to 3 percent effective December 9.

The central bank now expects inflation to exceed 9 percent before returning to the target 5 percent in late 2027.

“Before eight days had even passed after the President presented 2027 economic forecasts to Parliament, the central bank raised interest rates and increased the country’s expenditure,” Karunanayake said.

He asked the Finance Minister to table both the August and November forecasts and clarify whether the central bank will submit a mandatory report under Section 26(5) of the Central Bank Act if inflation stays above 7 percent for two consecutive quarters.

Karunanayake pointed out that locking up 120 to 150 billion rupees of excess liquidity through the reserve ratio hike imposes a 12 billion rupee opportunity cost on commercial banks, while a 25-basis-point yield rise on 2,300 billion rupees in Treasury bills adds 5.75 billion rupees annually.

“If commercial banks take a 12 billion rupee hit, what is the impact on government debt servicing? I am sure this will go up by 150 to 200 billion,” he warned.

He questioned how struggling small and medium enterprises — still recovering from the Easter bombings and past 30 percent interest rates — can survive, and whether a 174 billion rupee concessionary loan target backed by just 64 billion rupees remains viable.

He also asked whether International Monetary Fund targets on net international reserves and inflation, alongside a looming US Federal Reserve rate hike, drove the decision. (Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: ADB trains Sri Lanka’s debt office on liability management, sovereign credit ratings
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The initiative is part of broader technical support to strengthen public debt administration and investor confidence.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Asian Development Bank (ADB) hosted a three-day training workshop in Colombo for Sri Lanka’s Public Debt Management Office (PDMO), central bank, and related state agencies to enhance expertise in liability management, investor relations, and sovereign credit ratings.

Directed by ADB Senior Treasury Specialists Daniel Heuberger and Dipika Darshani, the initiative is part of broader technical support to strengthen public debt administration and investor confidence.

The PDMO of the Ministry of Finance engaged in the workshop on liability management, investor engagement and sovereign credit ratings under the technical assistance of the ADB.

“The workshop forms part of ADB’s continued technical assistance to strengthen PDMO’s institutional and operational capacity, support effective public debt management, enhance investor confidence and contribute to Sri Lanka’s efforts to improve sovereign creditworthiness,” the ministry said. (Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s 1990 Suwa Seriya faces staffing crisis, empty CEO post over frozen salaries
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Employees recruited when the service began in 2016 still earn the exact same basic starting salary as newly hired staff
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s 1990 Suwa Seriya ambulance service is struggling with staff resignations and an 11-month vacancy for its Chief Executive Officer post because salaries have lacked annual increments since 2016 and top pay is capped at 200,000 rupees a month.

Officials told a parliamentary Committee on Public Enterprises (COPE) sub-committee that employees recruited when the service began in 2016 still earn the exact same basic starting salary as newly hired staff today.

Because the foundation lacks a formal Scheme of Recruitment approved by the Department of Management Services, workers have no promotion path, pension, or annual salary increments, Board Director Nalin Perera said.

“It is regrettable to state that 1990 Suwa Seriya is an institution where employees work without any annual salary increments,” Perera told lawmakers during the hearing.

During a recent public sector pay hike of around 60 percent, Suwa Seriya field workers received an increase of only 15,000 to 16,000 rupees, widening the pay gap and driving trained staff to leave for jobs abroad.

So far this year, 48 employees, including 28 Emergency Medical Technicians (EMTs), have resigned, following 22 EMT resignations last year, leaving a shortage of between 100 and 200 field personnel.

The pay structure has also crippled senior leadership recruitment, leaving the CEO position vacant for 11 months alongside several empty second-tier management posts.

“Qualified candidates expect between 1 million and 1.5 million rupees, and the only applicants at 200,000 rupees were retirees around 70 years old,” Chairman Niroshana Ratnayake said.

Treasury officials explained that because initial cadre and salary scales were approved directly by the Cabinet rather than the Department of Management Services, every recruitment or pay adjustment requires fresh Cabinet approval.

Lawmakers urged the foundation and the Ministry of Health to fast-track a Cabinet paper to formalize the recruitment scheme, establish annual increments, and hire between 450 and 900 new staff needed for 150 incoming ambulances next year. (Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: Central Bank says 70-pct gold loan cap limits risks as pawning grows
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Pawning has grown alongside personal loans, consumption credit, and financial services as overall credit expanded by 25%
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka Central Bank Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said a 70 percent loan-to-value limit on gold loans has helped protect both banks and borrowers as pawning expands alongside rising gold prices and strong overall credit growth.

“That’s why, prudentially, it’s good that we imposed the loan-to-value ratio of 70%, to minimize the risk of those loans — not only for the customer, but also for the bank,” Weerasinghe said.

Responding to a question on financial pressure facing ordinary households, he noted that rising gold values allow people to borrow larger amounts against their gold, pushing up loan volumes.

If gold prices later drop, borrowers might feel it is not worth settling their loans, making the 70 percent cap a needed safeguard.

Pawning has grown alongside personal loans, consumption credit, and financial services as overall credit expanded by 25 percent, with some sectors naturally growing faster than others where new opportunities exist.

Weerasinghe said the trend was also raised by a board member at the Monetary Policy Committee meeting, but stressed that pawning serves a useful purpose for ordinary people, particularly farmers needing short-term money for cultivation.

“Because it’s the easiest way to take a loan—within 15 minutes they can walk into a bank and take it—that doesn’t mean that pawning is a bad thing,” he said.

He explained that pawning gives people without easy access to regular bank loans a fast way to borrow and repay after the harvest at reasonable rates compared to informal lenders.

Weerasinghe added that banks must answer for how they disburse credit, while interest rates target overall credit growth rather than curbing one sector, noting the 70 percent limit now appears to be the right measure.  (Colombo/Nov23/2026)

item.title: Central Bank does not target specific growth, focuses on inflation: Governor
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: "Our responsibility is to make sure the economy grows around its potential going forward. That is what monetary policy i
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Central Bank is not targeting a specific level of economic growth and remains focused on containing inflation as its main goal, Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said.

He made these remarks when asked by a journalist whether current policy rates could slow down economic growth heading into next year, and if the issue was discussed at the Monetary Board meeting.

“What is really important for us is containing inflation, which is our key objective. I don’t think the Central Bank is in the process of targeting a certain level of growth,” Weerasinghe said.

He explained that overall economic growth is shaped by many other policies, while the Central Bank’s role is to keep growth steady near its potential level.

“Our responsibility is to make sure the economy grows around its potential going forward. That is what monetary policy is all about,” he said.

While the Central Bank has not yet made an official growth forecast for next year, its internal models and technical analysis show that the economy is still growing close to its potential.

Weerasinghe added that although the bank’s analysis still shows a negative output gap this year, it hopes the economy will continue to grow around its potential next year as well. (Colombo/Nov21/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka central bank rejects claims account freezes stopped plantation payouts
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: ECONOMYNEXT – Claims that plantation companies cannot pay salaries or depositors because the Central Bank froze their accounts are completely false, Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said. Speaking to reporters, Weerasinghe said the Central Bank had frozen only a very small portion of the illegally collected deposits. A large portion had already been collected by the firms, […]
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Claims that plantation companies cannot pay salaries or depositors because the Central Bank froze their accounts are completely false, Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said.

Speaking to reporters, Weerasinghe said the Central Bank had frozen only a very small portion of the illegally collected deposits. A large portion had already been collected by the firms, and none of their plantations, agricultural projects, or other businesses have been banned.

He noted that if these firms truly earn around 40 percent returns from cultivation as claimed, freezing a small portion of accounts would not stop them from paying workers or repaying depositors.

“Saying that they cannot pay clearly demonstrates that these institutions can only be maintained if they collect money from the public again,” Weerasinghe said.

He urged the public not to fall for fraudulent deposit schemes disguised as legitimate businesses. Affected depositors should act according to their agreements and take legal steps quickly to recover their money, while existing court cases proceed in the prescribed manner and the Central Bank continues its own legal action to stop public deception.

Weerasinghe also condemned one or two individuals on social media who allegedly take money to spread false and vulgar personal attacks against senior Central Bank staff, particularly female officials.

While anyone is free to criticize central bank policies, he said the institution will always stand up for honest officials carrying out their duties properly.

“If they continue to do this, we will take specific legal action against them on behalf of the Central Bank,” he warned.

Weerasinghe thanked responsible media and genuine social media activists, adding that those making paid attacks have no credibility because they change sides depending on who pays them. (Colombo/November 20/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka-France Business Council to host wine evening, fashion show
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The evening is intended to serve as a networking platform for members of the local business community, partners, and fas
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Sri Lanka–France Business Council (SLFBC) of the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, with Modart International, will host its annual Wine Evening and Fashion Show in Colombo next week to promote bilateral cultural and commercial ties.

The event is scheduled to take place on November 26, from 6 pm onwards at the Cinnamon Grand Colombo, organizers said.

Beyond the fashion presentation, the evening is intended to serve as a networking platform for members of the local business community, partners, and fashion enthusiasts.

“Events such as these provide an opportunity to celebrate the cultural and creative dimensions of the relationship between Sri Lanka and France, while creating space for people from different sectors to connect,” SLFBC President Shaameel Mohideen said.

French Ambassador to Sri Lanka Rémi Lambert will attend as Chief Guest.

The runway showcase will feature collections inspired by the design traditions and craftsmanship of French fashion houses, paired with a curated selection of fine wines.

The initiative reflects its ongoing efforts to strengthen ties between the two countries through creative and cultural engagement alongside traditional trade and investment activities, the council said. (Colombo/Nov21/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka plugs $50,000 import advance loophole as banks, Customs tighten checks
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: CB is currently investigating the outflows, which took place under an earlier circular issued by the Import and Export C
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Central Bank and police have uncovered a large-scale foreign exchange abuse in which individuals repeatedly sent $50,000 import advance payments out of the country through multiple banks without bringing in goods, prompting tougher rules, a cross-bank tracking system, and heavy fines.

Central Bank Governor Nandalal Weerasinghe said the Department of Foreign Exchange is currently investigating the outflows, which took place under an earlier circular issued by the Import and Export Control Department of the Ministry of Finance.

Wider $1 billion outflow probe

The Central Bank’s findings come amid a broader investigation into illicit dollar outflows.

In June 2026, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake told Parliament that authorities were probing around US$1 billion (about Rs. 300 billion) sent out of Sri Lanka since 2023 via Telegraphic Transfers (TT) as import advances without any goods arriving in return.

Dissanayake said the outflows involved money linked to drugs, corruption, and organized crime, and alleged that certain bank branches and bank managers were involved in the transactions, continuing the schemes even after moving to other banks.

How the $50,000 advance loophole worked

Under the earlier Ministry of Finance circular, importers were allowed to obtain an advance payment of up to $50,000 by presenting an invoice at a commercial bank.

Once remitted, the transaction is recorded in Sri Lanka Customs’ ASYCUDA system, and the importer must bring the goods into the country within 180 days.

If the goods do not arrive within six months, Customs is responsible for notifying the Central Bank’s Department of Foreign Exchange so legal action can be taken against non-BOI entities for violating foreign exchange laws.

However, Customs had failed to provide this data to the Central Bank for a long time despite repeated requests.

The full scale of the abuse only emerged after authorities received tips that individuals were using the facility continuously, prompting a police investigation.

Investigators found that huge amounts of dollars had been sent abroad in $50,000 advances without goods arriving within six months, with some transactions never even recorded at Customs.

“Some action had been taken regarding the ones that were notified, but it was only later discovered that the number of unnotified cases was massive,” Governor Weerasinghe said.

Multiple banks and shell companies

Checks at commercial banks revealed that the same individuals were visiting different bank branches under the names of different companies to obtain repeated $50,000 advances.

Because banks had to release the funds when presented with an invoice — and non-arrival could only be verified after 180 days — the scheme went undetected for months.

“When an invoice is brought in, what was discovered is that the very same person had come to certain bank branches representing different companies,” he said.

Tighter rules and legal action

To close the loophole, authorities have introduced stricter rules on import advance payments, including requiring a Tax Identification Number (TIN) when requesting an advance.

The Import and Export Control Department has also issued new regulations requiring thorough background checks before funds are released.

“Who the importer is, who their beneficial owner is, what the company is, whether they have prior records—it is only after checking all of those things that it is done now,” Governor Weerasinghe said.

A new mechanism has also been introduced allowing commercial banks to check whether an applicant has already obtained an advance payment from another bank.

Law enforcement agencies have treated the cases as fraud and initiated legal action alongside regulatory penalties.

Enforcement is being carried out under two tracks: the Import and Export Control Department handles violations involving BOI companies, while the Central Bank’s Department of Foreign Exchange takes legal action against non-BOI entities once reported by Customs.

Governor Weerasinghe said fines have already been imposed on a large number of companies involved in both the earlier reported cases and the additional cases uncovered later. (Colombo/Nov21/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka central bank to get marketable bonds next year to mop up liquidity
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: "The Treasury bond stock is going to be replaced with plain vanilla instruments from March next year," Amarasekara said.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s central bank will gain a large stock of marketable Treasury bonds starting March next year, giving it a market-based tool to permanently absorb excess cash in the banking system without issuing its own securities, Deputy Governor Chandranath Amarasekara said.

The shift will happen once a temporary “step-down” interest rate feature on the central bank’s restructured government bond holdings expires in March, converting them into standard fixed-rate bonds — known in financial markets as “plain vanilla” instruments — carrying a 5 percent coupon.

“The Treasury bond stock is going to be replaced with plain vanilla instruments from March next year,” Amarasekara said.

“For the remaining maturity, it will be fixed at 5 percent,” he said.

Until now, commercial banks and investors have avoided these step-down bonds because their changing interest rates made them difficult to price.

Once they carry a fixed 5 percent rate, the central bank will be able to sell them at a discount so their yields match market rates, allowing authorities to drain excess rupees after assessing investor appetite.

The bond stock dates back to 2020, when the central bank purchased large volumes of Treasury bills — effectively printing money and cutting interest rates — to close a potential gap in economic output.

During Sri Lanka’s debt restructuring, those Treasury bills were converted into long-term government bonds with lower step-down interest rates for the first two to three years.

Amarasekara was responding to questions on why the monetary authority does not issue its own long-term securities to absorb excess cash instead of raising bank reserve requirements, which act as a de facto tax on commercial banks as they are unremunerated in Sri Lanka. (Colombo/Nov21/2026)

item.title: Digital microlending in ‘regulatory black hole’, Sri Lanka think tank finds
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Highlighting the need for enhancing digital literacy and consumer protection enforcement
item.content:encoded:
Micro loans being promoted via text messages and social media are opaque and predatory, and risk misleading vulnerable borrowers, according to a new report by Centre for a Smart Future.

In a new flagship report, ‘Fast Cash, Hidden Risks: Digital Microloans in Sri Lanka’, the Colombo-based think tank called for better regulation of these lending service providers, currently “falling in a regulatory black hole”.

CSF argues that these digital microloans have proliferated among vulnerable communities in the aftermath of the economic crisis and rising pressures on the household budget, but little has been known about how they operate, who they affect, and what risks are borne by borrowers.

The report has revealed how these digital lending services use misleading and predatory advertising, and opaque terms of use, to lure in borrowers, with problematic collection techniques and hidden costs. The report reveals instances of harassment faced by borrowers, which the gap in regulation has allowed these services to go unchecked.

Furthermore, concerns are raised about personal data privacy as digital loan apps request numerous permissions on users’ mobile devices, including access to call logs and contacts, photos, and other information.

The report observes that, per Sri Lanka’s Personal Data Protection Act, the requirements for these permissions are not sufficiently explained in digital microloan providers’ policies, nor is it sufficiently explained what data is collected through them and what the data will be used for, or what third parties they will be shared with.

Despite all this, users of digital microloans say that these companies provide a necessary service which banks cannot offer, covering short-term shortfall or emergency expenses, especially for those who are excluded from the traditional banking system.

They recognise that, with more transparency and fairer repayment terms, it would be a valuable system.

However, digital microloan providers exist in a regulatory black hole. The report emphasizes that there is no existing institution that would be able to regulate these companies as they do not come under the mandate of the Central Bank, which only governs deposit taking institutions.

The newly enacted Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Act has the potential to regulate digital lenders, but the authority which would oversee enforcement has not yet been established. The Act is also reportedly being amended, which may lead to further delays.

Combining qualitative interviews with a deep-dive review of the major digital microloan providers in Sri Lanka the new report aims to outline who uses these services and what for, how these companies operate and promote their services, and what risks are faced by borrowers.

CSF has provided recommendations for better coordination between regulators, data protection authorities, cybercrime agencies, and law enforcement, as well as highlighting the need for enhancing digital literacy and consumer protection enforcement, especially to help vulnerable populations.

The full report is available at csf-asia.org/digital-microloans-study. (Colombo/Nov21/2026)
